title: A death in custody leaves haunting questions
subtitle: Man who died in holding cell was left alone for nine hours
article: There were signs Bradley Prebble's health was failing within minutes of his arrival at a Scarborough police station. The 48-year-old was unsteady on his feet. He told booking officers he was experiencing numbness and had pain in his eye, hand and foot. During a pat down, he'd moaned in agony when a cop touched his swollen right ankle.

But the father and TTC employee wasn't offered medical attention while being booked into custody for assault, and he didn't request it. Instead, surveillance video inside 43 Division captured him slowly wobble to his holding cell before dinnertime on Oct. 13, 2021.

By morning, Prebble was dead. His body was found in his cell, where he'd laid unmoving for nearly five hours before anyone came in, according to a summary of surveillance video by Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU).
By the time he was discovered, rigor mortis, the muscle stiffening that begins several hours after death, had already set in.

"Paramedics were summoned to the scene and determined there was nothing that could be done to revive him," SIU director Joseph Martino, wrote in a 2022 report on Prebble's death, which a coroner later ruled was caused by complications from alcoholism, according to police.
"It was evident that (Prebble) had been deceased for some time."
Whether Prebble might be alive today if police followed their own prisoner safety protocol is the question now haunting Prebble's grieving family.
Grief over his death is compounded by anger and confusion over how he was left alone for nearly nine hours when police are required to physically check on prisoners about every 30 minutes.

"They were supposed to check on him, and nobody came," Cathy Prebble, Bradley's mother, said through tears in an interview from her home in Prince Edward County. "He could possibly still be alive if somebody had checked on him."

The SIU, which probes deaths and serious injuries involving police, cleared the senior officer supervising the cells of any criminal offence but uncovered "indiscretions" by booking officers tasked with monitoring Prebble. Those included an erroneous claim by a special constable that he'd checked on Prebble and saw him sitting up in his cell at 4:16 a.m., which was disproven by cell video. But the booking officers were special constables - civilian employees not bound by Ontario policing laws - meaning the SIU had "no statutory jurisdiction to investigate."
"The matter of their conduct in connection with (Prebble's) time in custody will be referred to (Toronto police)," the SIU said.

In a report to the Toronto police board last June, then Toronto police chief James Ramer confirmed five employees - two staff sergeants and three civilian "special constables" - failed to comply with a procedure requiring that officers enter a prisoner's cell about twice an hour. The sergeants were placed under investigation by the professional standards unit to determine if misconduct charges were warranted, while the conduct of the civilian special constables was "being managed by Labour Relations," the report stated.
But Toronto police won't say what came of their internal investigation, including if any employees were disciplined.

Police spokesperson Stephanie Sayer told the Star the force is legally prohibited from releasing details about misconduct investigations unless the matter results in a disciplinary hearing, which didn't happen in Prebble's case. Meanwhile, the force won't comment on any "private human resources matter" involving special constables.
"We would offer our condolences to the family for their loss," Sayer said in an email.

Prebble's family has filed a lawsuit against the Toronto police board, Ramer and the officers involved, alleging police were "recklessly indifferent" to Prebble's welfare. They allege police denied Prebble much-needed medical attention upon his arrival and then ignored signs of distress throughout the night; in his final hours, surveillance video showed Prebble fidgeting in the cell, hanging over the toilet and taking his clothing off and putting it on, according to the SIU's investigation.

"Proper checks may have saved Brad's life," said Ed Upenieks, the civil lawyer representing Prebble's family in the lawsuit. "It is simply unacceptable for any person in custody not to be checked for nine hours, in particular those like Brad with readily apparent health issues."
No statement of defence has yet been filed. Sayer said Toronto police will be filing a defence and declined to comment further while the case was before the courts.

According to the SIU, Prebble arrived at Toronto police 43 division around 3 p.m. on Oct. 13, 2021, following a 911 call from a motel on Scarborough's Kingston Road reporting an alleged domestic disturbance between Prebble and a 35-year-old woman. He was arrested for assault and failing to comply with the terms of his release.

Soon after, he complained to booking officers about numerous health issues, including numbness, bruising and balance problems, but said he'd talked to a pharmacist about the ailments and wasn't concerned. He was soon led into a cell and "walked slowly and was unsteady on his feet," the SIU report says.

Surveillance video, which has no audio, then showed Prebble in the cell and police checking in. Around 8:41 p.m., Prebble began to "appear restless," the SIU report said. He hung over the cell toilet before knocking on the window and waving at the cell camera, prompting a booking officer to remove Prebble from the cell and place him in another across the hall.

At 11:13 p.m., a booking officer opened Prebble's door, took him out of the cell, then returned him by 11:21. According to the SIU's timeline of cell video, this was the last time officers physically checked on Prebble.

Over the next few hours, Prebble removed articles of clothing and then put them back on. He took his shoe and sock off his swollen right ankle and rolled up his pant leg. He alternated between laying on the cell bench and fidgeting while sitting, the SIU report said.
At 3:32 a.m., video captured Prebble suddenly flinch while lying down. It was his final movement on the motion-activated video.
No one entered the cell until 8:13 a.m. when a booking officer attempted to rouse Prebble and found him dead.
Officers attempted chest compressions and called paramedics who determined Prebble couldn't be revived.

Martino, the director of the SIU, said, given his ill health upon arrival, it "might perhaps have been advisable" to send Prebble to the hospital, but the failure to do so was not a "marked departure" from a reasonable level of care.

Although he cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing, Martino raised questions about Prebble's in-custody supervision, particularly after 3:30 a.m. when he was entirely motionless. One booking officer claimed he'd checked on Prebble at 4:16 a.m. and observed him sitting up - "that would not appear to have been the case," Martino wrote. Another recorded multiple checks on Prebble via the cell door windows and the video monitors and said Prebble seemed to be sleeping and was not in distress.
"It is apparent (Prebble) was not sleeping for at least some of these checks, if not all of them - he was experiencing an acute medical episode or was deceased," Martino wrote.
Prebble's grieving relatives have experienced differing emotions when it comes to his death in police custody.

For Jeffrey Prebble, Bradley's brother, it's anger - that Brad isn't around to raise his young daughter, that he can no longer reminisce about childhood with his sibling and that Toronto police, he believes, haven't owned up to what went wrong.
"It's unacceptable, it cannot happen again," he said. "I want the problem dealt with and there should be repercussions because of it."

For Cathy, her son's death has her stuck in "terrible grief." She'd been close to Bradley, their bond increasing after the sudden death of Bradley's 10-year-old son in 2006 of epilepsy. The two often went out for breakfast and could sit and talk for hours, something she felt her son often needed. She deeply misses his companionship, she said.
"I cry at the drop of a hat - it's like an open wound, it doesn't close, it doesn't heal," she said. "Because I have so many questions and I have no answers."
CREDIT: Wendy Gillis Toronto Star
